title: The way, the truth, the life (III.56)
hookLine: without the way there's no going
tomorrow: why would anyone hesitate at a door they're invited through?

lines: A RIDDLE YOU CAN WALK WITH.
cards: No route found. The little gray words when the map app gives up: no road, or no signal, or a place too far off the grid. What do you do then?
Usually, shake the phone. Near the end of book three, the Imitation answers with a sentence from the Gospel of John, and then folds it into a Latin riddle short enough to say while you walk.

teach.h: I AM THE WAY, THE TRUTH, THE LIFE.
teach.b: The sentence comes first. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says it at the supper table: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." Chapter fifty-six has Christ quote it to the disciple, and then the riddle.
Without the way, there is no going. Without the truth, there is no knowing. Without the life, there is no living.
In Latin the first part is three tiny words: sine via non itur. Notice it maps onto a stalled trip.

teach.h: ROAD, MAP AND STRENGTH: ONE PERSON.
teach.b: No road, no map, no strength to step, and the chapter says all three are one person. Then it gives each a job. I am the way to be followed, Christ says, the truth to be believed, the life to be hoped for.

teach.h: GO OUT OF YOURSELF TO ENTER.
teach.b: And the cost, stated plainly: as far as you can go out of yourself, that far you can enter into me. Here's the thing worth repeating: a way isn't something you admire from a bench.
You only know a road by walking it. So the chapter's answer to no route found isn't a better map. It's a companion who is also the road.

how: Catholics hear John 14:6 at funerals and on feasts, and the Way of the Cross, walked from station to station in many churches, is one way the faith turns following Christ into actual steps.

o: a set of rules to learn before you can pray
Christ as the road itself: without him, no going
a pilgrimage route walked once in a lifetime

p: and you can enter into me

s: "I am the way" in the Imitation means a rulebook to study first
the chapter's way is someone to follow, walked by going out of yourself.
the riddle's Latin begins sine via non itur
without the way, there is no going.
the chapter says you must know the whole road before you start
the way is followed; the truth believed; the life hoped for. a road is known by walking it.

games.q: your friend wants to start praying but says she'll wait until she understands all of it first. what does the Imitation's riddle suggest?
o: start walking; the way is known by following, not by studying first.
she's right: without the truth there's no knowing, so read first.
skip both; the life matters, not the way or the truth.
games.why: the chapter keeps all three together, but the way is something you follow. you learn a road by walking it.

practice: Stand up and take a slow walk, across the room or down a hall, for the length of the sit; if you can't stand, let each breath be a step. Feel your heel, then your toes, touch the floor.
Say one word with each step: way, truth, life.

wordCard.voice: The way. Christ's name for himself in John, and the Imitation's riddle: without the way, there's no going anywhere at all.

orig.note: Latin, Imitation III.56: without the way, there is no going.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the way, not a map in a drawer but someone to walk beside. Book four opens tomorrow.
